Senses.Explanation: To descend from the teaching seat. In the Chan record this is the standard visible close of a formal teaching-seat appearance: the person who mounted the seat may finish speaking, shout, strike or plant an implement, remain silent, or answer a demand by leaving. The action is not interchangeable with the preceding speech. Shakyamuni Buddha descends after Manjusri's sounding-block declaration in one Five Lamps scene and after his own refusal to preach in another. Tianyi Yihuai shouts and descends; Feiyin Tongrong descends only after the chief seat gives the closing declaration; and Langting Jingting says of passing geese, “They have passed,” before descending. Yaoshan Weiyan mounts the seat, remains silent, descends, and only afterward answers the rector in his quarters. When Zhaozhou Congshen asks Nanquan Puyuan to speak apart from the four propositions and hundred negations, Nanquan descends and returns to his quarters. The Linji Yixuan–Mayu Baoche exchange makes the actors especially important: Mayu first pulls Linji down and takes the seat, Linji then pulls Mayu down and retakes it, and Linji finally descends after Mayu leaves. Juelang Daosheng is preparing to descend when a lay questioner introduced as Huang Gong tells him, “Please step down.” These formal endings, commands, and forcible removals all preserve the same concrete movement away from the seat.

Senses.Explanation: A rare nominal use for the lower of two seating positions, rather than the act of descending. In a Complete Collection of the Five Lamps encounter, Censor Wang first asks whether the bow is southern or northern and then whether it is from the upper or lower seat. Senses.Explanation: To step down from the teaching seat is a visible move in a public encounter. Xiuxi descends and is seized after two steps; Zhaozhou descends to inspect a questioner; Yungai Zhi descends and spreads his hands to Jiufeng; Baizhang Weizheng separately descends and spreads his hands after the community requests the promised teaching. The movement is part of each answer, not the ending of an ordinary sitting session.

The headword names the act and product of submitting an on-the-spot response for judgment on a case or challenge. Compiler narration records assemblies, many people, or a senior monk submitting responses; those participants perform the response but do not utter the recorder-governed verb. Langye Huijue gives his own final response, while other records narrate failed group responses, ordered responses, ninety-six unsuccessful attempts, and Nanyue Huairang’s eventual answer ‘to call it a thing misses.’ Acceptance, rejection, replacement, and renewed challenge concern one public response operation rather than separate noun and verb senses.

Seven witnesses across five independent works meet the packet floor and cover assembly response, final response, failed group responses, ordered response, repeated attempts, reported failure, and delayed successful submission.

SearchAliases: look at the word or saying
Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes look at the word or saying in these Chan records. Its wording is ‘look at the talk’: look at the word, saying, question, or conversational thread singled out in a record. The compound most often occurs in ‘look at the saying's head’ (看話頭), and the local wording—not an imported technical label—determines whether English says word, saying, question, or thread. The records include the recorded questioner seeking written direction because the saying he was looking at had not opened to him. They also preserve criticism: Mingben reports people calling looking at a saying ‘doing work’ and rejects their appeal to direct transmission; Yuancheng says an old hunter neither did work nor looked at a saying before answering that there was ‘no place to set a hand,’ and contrasts this with looking left and right at one's own selected saying. Another record demands, ‘if you recognize it and can say it, come out and say it—what does the end of the talk say?’ Thus the Zen deviation is an ordinary act of looking directed at actual words in recorded exchanges and itself subjected to criticism in the record.
